title: Synthesizing Property & Casualty Ratemaking Datasets using Generative Adversarial Networks
summary: Compares three GAN architectures for producing shareable property and casualty ratemaking data, judging each on whether it reproduces the original data structure and the predictive models fitted to it, on privacy, and on how hard it is to use in practice, demonstrated on the public French motor third-party liability dataset. CTGAN is one of the three architectures actually run, given its own section and applied following Kuo's ratemaking adaptation, and the paper's practitioner-facing conclusion is that CTGAN is the easiest of the three to use while MC-WGAN-GP synthesizes the best data.
evidence: the abstract states that to reflect the characteristics of insurance data the authors use GAN architectures adapted for multicategorical data, naming a Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty (MC-WGAN-GP), a conditional tabular GAN (CTGAN), and a mixed numerical and categorical differentially private GAN, illustrated on the French motor third-party liability data, and reports as a headline finding that MC-WGAN-GP synthesizes the best data, the CTGAN is the easiest to use, and the MNCDP-GAN guarantees differential privacy; section 3 is devoted to CTGAN, opening that another possible path to simulating insurance claim data is through a conditional tabular GAN or CTGAN (L. Xu et al. 2019), noting the method was applied to ratemaking data in Kuo (2019) and that Kuo developed an R wrapper for it; the same section describes the training-by-sampling procedure in operation, stating that following Kuo the authors use the true data frequency to sample the conditioning value rather than the log-frequency suggested in Xu et al.

title: Leveraging Large Language Models and GAN-Augmented Data for Energy Load Prediction
summary: Proposes DAPM-LLM, which converts residential building energy records into natural-language prompts so that a fine-tuned Bart model can predict energy usage, and pairs that with a tabular augmentation module because the source dataset holds only 768 samples. The augmentation is not SDV: the authors run Ashrapov's TabGan library, and CTGAN appears only in the survey of tabular GANs and in a background subsection crediting Xu et al. with mode-specific normalization for multimodal and non-Gaussian columns.
evidence: the related-work section states that the inability of Table-GAN to regulate synthetic data creation may exacerbate imbalances in categorical features and that the Conditional Tabular GAN (CTGAN) and SMOTE have been introduced to solve these issues, citing Xu et al. 2019 as reference 31; a background subsection headed Conditional Tabular GAN describes CTGAN as a GAN-based technique that samples rows from a tabular data distribution to model it, and credits Xu et al. with developing mode-specific normalization to address multimodal and non-Gaussian distribution challenges; the methodology states that many libraries and methods are available for tabular data augmentation and that in this work the authors used the TabGan library provided by Ashrapov, which offers GAN, conditional GAN and diffusion methods, selecting GAN and CGAN from it. No CTGAN row appears in any results table and the SDV implementation is not run

title: Generative Adversarial Networks in Actuarial Modeling- Enhancing Predictions of Long-Tail Risks Done
summary: Argues that long-tail insurance risks are hard to price because the historical record contains too few severe events, and surveys how adversarial generation could synthesize rare-event representations to fill that gap, with a Wasserstein-style stabilization for the training dynamics. CTGAN is cited twice as the reference point for tabular adversarial generation and nothing more: the paper credits Xu et al. with preserving statistical attributes of tabular data while noting they did not address rare events, and misnames the model TabGAN in doing so.
evidence: the introduction states that GANs have demonstrated exceptional capability in generating synthetic data retaining the statistical characteristics of training datasets across multiple domains, citing Xu et al. 2019 as reference 7, and argues this makes them suited to synthesizing rare events; the related-work section states that while GANs have been widely used in image synthesis their application to tabular data remains relatively underexplored, and that Xu et al. (2019) introduced TabGAN for generating synthetic tabular datasets, showing the method preserved key statistical attributes but did not specifically address the challenge of modeling rare events; reference 7 resolves to Xu, Skoularidou, Cuesta-Infante and Veeramachaneni, Modeling tabular data using conditional GAN. The name TabGAN is the paper's own error for CTGAN, and no CTGAN implementation is run or benchmarked anywhere in the paper

title: SAEDF: A Synthetic Anomaly-Enhanced Detection Framework for Detection of Unknown Network Attacks
summary: Targets zero-day network attacks, which signature-based intrusion detection cannot see, by synthesizing anomalous traffic to enlarge the space of attacks a detector has been exposed to, built on adaptive generative variational components rather than on a tabular GAN. CTGAN contributes a technique rather than a model: the framework's preprocessing employs the specialized normalization CTGAN introduced, to handle mixed continuous and categorical traffic features while preserving their distributions, but CTGAN itself is neither run nor benchmarked.

evidence: the preprocessing section states that feature scales vary widely and that uniformity in data representation is critical for model performance, and that to address this variability the specialized normalization technique introduced in CTGAN, reference 38, was employed; the same passage states the method demonstrated considerable effectiveness in managing mixed-type data by normalizing continuous variables and encoding categorical variables while maintaining their intrinsic distributions and relationships; the generative component of the framework is described as adaptive and dynamic generative variational, not a conditional tabular GAN, and no CTGAN row appears in any results table. This is the adopted-but-not-run pattern: CTGAN's mode-specific normalization is implemented inside the pipeline while the model is absent

title: Machine Learning Approach for Iron Deficiency Anemia Detection in Pregnant Women Using XGBoost and CTGAN
summary: Builds a screening model for iron deficiency anemia in pregnancy from 3,944 anonymized clinical records, taking trimester-specific shifts in hematological reference ranges into account rather than applying a single threshold, and optimizing for sensitivity because a missed case matters more than a false alarm. CTGAN is half the named method and is run to correct the class imbalance between anemic and non-anemic records, with the paper's stated hypothesis being that an XGBoost model optimized with CTGAN-corrected training data outperforms conventional complete-blood-count screening.
evidence: the title names CTGAN as one of the two methods, and the abstract states the study introduces a machine learning framework integrating Extreme Gradient Boosting and Conditional Tabular Generative Adversarial Networks (CTGAN) for early detection of iron deficiency anemia in pregnant women, addressing the class imbalance inherent in clinical datasets while incorporating trimester-specific hematological adaptations across 3,944 records; the background states that clinical datasets exhibit significant class imbalance with non-anemic cases far outnumbering anemic ones, which can severely compromise model sensitivity, and that generative models, particularly CTGAN, offer a mechanism for synthesizing realistic minority-class samples to balance skewed datasets, citing Xu et al. 2019; the stated hypothesis is that an AI model optimized with CTGAN for class imbalance and trained on pregnancy-specific hematological data will significantly improve detection performance over conventional screening

title: GOGGLE: Generative Modelling for Tabular Data by Learning Relational Structure
summary: Argues that tabular generative models ignore the dependency structure among columns, and proposes GOGGLE, which learns a relational graph over variables and generates each variable conditioned on its learned neighbourhood through a message-passing network inside a variational autoencoder, so the generative process is explicit about which variables depend on which. Three SDV-family models are among the benchmarks: CTGAN and CopulaGAN appear in the model-class taxonomy and CTGAN and TVAE carry rows in the quality and detection tables across the UCI datasets.
evidence: the model-class table lists CopulaGAN, TableGAN and CTGAN as GAN/MLP neural methods and TVAE as a VAE/MLP method, against GOGGLE as VAE/MPNN, scoring each on whether it makes the generative factorization, the relational structure and the conditional independencies explicit; the benchmarks paragraph states the authors compare against state-of-the-art tabular synthetic data models including Bayesian networks and the GAN-based CTGAN and TableGAN, the VAE-based TVAE and normalising flows, following the experiment design in Xu et al. and using eight UCI datasets plus two further ones; the quality table reports CTGAN and TVAE scores on Adult, Breast, Covertype and Credit against GOGGLE, and the detection table repeats the comparison. GOGGLE's generator is a message-passing VAE, so CTGAN's conditional vector is benchmarked rather than adopted

title: Handling Uncertainty in Health Data using Generative Algorithms
summary: Proposes RIGA, which converts small imbalanced clinical tables into image representations so that image generative models can augment them, then converts back for tabular classifiers, tested on a preterm-birth cohort and a myocardial infarction dataset where the minority class is very small. CTGAN is the tabular augmentation baseline the image route is measured against, reported as reducing AUC on some datasets and giving a modest 0.87 per cent improvement on another, and named as the tabular GAN the authors' approach outperforms.
evidence: the related-work section states that GANs have been used to augment tabular data but their popularity is limited by challenges with mixed numerical and categorical features, that Conditional Tabular GAN (Xu et al. 2019) adapts to tabular data by normalizing mixed features and has been found to outperform other GAN-based methods, and that the authors' approach outperforms CTGAN, suggesting converting tabular data to images is productive; the nuMoM2b results state that ADASYN and SMOTE decreased XGBoost AUC while CTGAN provided minimal improvement; the myocardial results state ADASYN, SMOTE and CTGAN reduced AUC scores; a further dataset reports that CTGAN, by leveraging adversarial training, provided a modest improvement of 0.87 per cent, showing its ability to capture more meaningful feature distributions; Table 1 carries an XGBoost and CTGAN row across the datasets

title: A Generalized Theory of Mixup for Structure-Preserving Synthetic Data
summary: Works out what mixup does to the moments of a dataset, showing that the usual interpolation shrinks the covariance and biases the expectation, and derives a mixing-weight distribution whose synthetic samples preserve both, which turns a heuristic augmentation into one with a stated structural guarantee. CTGAN and TVAE are the deep generative baselines the theory is checked against empirically, run from the synthcity open-source implementations, and the bias tables show CTGAN substantially disturbing the covariance and expectation that the proposed scheme preserves.
evidence: the introduction places variational autoencoders and generative adversarial networks for tabular data in the lineage it works against, citing Xu et al. 2019 for both; the experimental section states the authors evaluate on tabular datasets using three mixup methods and four baseline methods available in open-source code from Qian et al. 2023, naming TVAE, CTGAN (Xu et al., 2019), TabDDPM and GReaT; the bias tables report per-moment bias for CTGAN across the datasets, and the discussion states that the ML-based synthetic datasets, CTGAN and TabDDPM, substantially disturb the covariance and expectation while the proposed EpBeta generates the most balanced synthetic data; the bibliography also carries CTAB-GAN and CTAB-GAN+ as further points in the same lineage

title: MALLM-GAN: Multi-Agent Large Language Model as Generative Adversarial Network for Synthesizing Tabular Data
summary: Casts synthetic tabular generation as a conversation between language-model agents playing generator and discriminator roles, so that a causal structure can be proposed and criticised in natural language rather than learned from scratch, which is aimed squarely at the scarce-data regime where conventional deep generators overfit. CTGAN and TVAE are two of the state-of-the-art baselines run against it, and the evaluation protocol itself, machine-learning efficiency alongside distance to closest record, is taken from Xu et al.
evidence: the introduction states that prior approaches run from Bayesian networks and oversampling through to deep learning techniques citing Xu et al. 2019, and that these methods require sufficient data for training which makes them overfit and under-representative on scarce data; the related-work section states that deep generative models such as VAEs (TVAE, Xu et al. 2019), GANs (CTGAN, Xu et al. 2019) and diffusion models have become dominant; the experimental setup states the authors compare MALLM-GAN with several state-of-the-art tabular generative models, naming SMOTE, TVAE, CTGAN, Be-GReaT, TabDDPM and Tabsyn; the evaluation section states the models are assessed on privacy leakage by distance to closest record and machine learning efficiency, citing Xu et al. 2019 for the protocol, and the results tables carry CTGAN and TVAE rows across Adult, Insurance, ATACH and ERICH at N=25

title: Do we need rebalancing strategies? A theoretical and empirical study around SMOTE and its variants
summary: Analyses SMOTE and its descendants theoretically, showing where interpolation-based oversampling does and does not help, and pairs that with a broad empirical comparison that includes the case of applying no rebalancing at all, arguing that the default assumption in favour of rebalancing is weaker than practice suggests. CTGAN is run as the deep generative arm of that comparison and is described in its own subsection, with the study reporting that it performs significantly worse than applying no strategy at all on three of the datasets.
affiliations: Artelys (France); Laboratoire de Probabilités et Modèles Aléatoires; Laboratoire de Probabilités, Statistique et Modélisation
Laboratoire de Probabilités et Modèles Aléatoires; Laboratoire de Probabilités, Statistique et Modélisation
evidence: the introduction states that other approaches to rebalancing are based on generative adversarial networks, citing Xu et al. 2019, or diffusion, and that these are computationally expensive and mostly designed for specific data structures; a subsection headed CTGAN and ForestDiff states that CTGAN (Conditional Tabular GAN) (Xu et al., 2019) is a conditional generative adversarial network specially designed for generating new synthetic samples for tabular datasets and that it uses conditional generation; the supplementary results state that CTGAN performances are significantly lower than those of the None strategy on three data sets while ForestDiffusion is among the best strategies for most data sets, with Table 2 carrying the CTGAN rows; the related-work discussion notes that an earlier claim that no rebalancing performs well excluded deep-learning-based oversampling methods such as CTGAN
